extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Congress members, congressional staff, administrative law policymakers, agency officials, and administrative law scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and reform the federal informal (notice-and-comment) rulemaking process: diagnose causes and pathologies (ossification), identify how agencies currently comply or avoid rules, and propose legislative and administrative fixes to restore timely, transparent, and effective rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice of proposed rulemaking requirements (§553(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must provide a 'general notice' of proposed rulemaking containing: '(1) a statement of the time, place, and nature of public rulemaking proceedings; (2) reference to the legal authority under which the rule is proposed; and (3) either the terms of substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline for adequate notice; evaluate whether the notice actually informs the public of the rule's substance, legal basis, and opportunities for participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for public participation (§553(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: After issuing the notice of proposed rulemaking, the agency must 'give interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rulemaking through submissions of written data, views, or arguments with or without opportunity for oral presentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the agency provided meaningful avenues for written and, where appropriate, oral input; consider whether procedural choices effectively excluded stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise general statement of basis and purpose for final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After considering comments, the agency must 'incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the final rule preamble explains the factual and policy bases sufficiently to permit meaningful judicial review and public understanding; attention to 'reasoned explanation' expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious judicial review standard (§706(2)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must 'hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings and conclusions found to be . . . arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard to determine when a rule should be set aside; note tension between accountability and over-intrusive review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-look (Motor Vehicle Manufacturers v. State Farm) four-part review test
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should set aside a rule if 'the agency has relied on factors which Congress has not intended it to consider; entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem; offered an explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency; or is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four subtests to judge the sufficiency of agency explanations and the administrative record; acknowledge variability across circuits and the risk of judicial overreaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality threshold for responding to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must rationally respond to outside comments that pass a 'threshold of materiality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether agencies identified and responded to materially significant comments; consider how 'threshold of materiality' is applied and whether it invites exhaustive (and costly) responses to every attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rulemaking via adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may make policy through individual adjudications instead of rulemaking, which deprives regulatees and beneficiaries of notice and a chance to influence policy and reduces public/Congressional accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess when agencies improperly use adjudication to create de facto rules; consider notice and opportunity-to-comment deficits and impacts on predictability and reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rulemaking via nonrule rulemaking (guidance, manuals, policy statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies increasingly use guidance documents, technical manuals, policy statements, and interim final rules not subject to comment as a way to avoid burdensome rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether such instruments are being used to implement substantive policy without proper notice-and-comment protections and whether they create reliance uncertainty due to lower-level issuance and lack of permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim final rule misuse and 'good cause' exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies often invoke the vague 'good cause' exception to make interim final rules effective immediately and then may never finalize them, producing de facto permanent rules without full notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether an interim final rule was justified by genuine urgency, whether the agency actually treated subsequent comments seriously, and whether statutes (or amendments) should require automatic expiration if not finalized (e.g., three-year expiration proposal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of supplemental analytical requirements (RIAs, Regulatory Flexibility Analyses, Unfunded Mandates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes and executive orders have added extensive analytical requirements—Regulatory Impact Analyses for major rules, Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses for effects on small businesses, Unfunded Mandates analyses—making rulemaking resource-intensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the marginal benefits of these analyses outweigh their costs for particular rulemakings; consider selectively reducing or tailoring these mandates to improve timeliness without sacrificing useful information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource-intensity and cost of developing comprehensive records and RIAs
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing comprehensive RIAs and administrative records for major rules can cost substantial staff time and consultant expense (often more than a million dollars for major efforts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor administrative cost, staff capacity, and opportunity costs into decisions about when and how extensively to prepare such analyses; weigh net public benefit of intensive analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized White House/OIRA review effects and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralized interagency review (OIRA) can exert significant control over substantive policy, slow rulemaking, and create incentives for agencies to avoid rulemaking; review lacks full transparency and may enable outside influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether OIRA input stays within appropriate analytic boundaries, whether transparency of OIRA-agency and outside-OIRA communications should be increased, and whether the review process chills protective regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of OIRA and outside lobbying during review
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of conversations between outside lobbyists and White House/OIRA officials about particular rulemaking initiatives are not generally disclosed, allowing potential undue influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider requiring public disclosure of OIRA-agency communications and communications between outside interests and OIRA/White House officials regarding specific rules to reduce abuse and increase accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional oversight should be systemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should step up systemic oversight of the rulemaking process, not limit inquiry to individual rules, using CRS and GAO to build a legislative record for reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rulemaking patterns across agencies and over time rather than only episodic investigations; use oversight to identify structural causes of ossification and to justify legislative fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate or narrow statutory and extra-statutory procedural mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could amend statutes (and presidents could limit executive orders) to remove marginal or duplicative procedural/analytical mandates that increase the burden of informal rulemaking and prompt agencies to avoid rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target mandates that add little value given their costs (e.g., reexamine Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements in certain contexts), clarifying when formal hearings are unnecessary under particular statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finalize interim final rules or require their expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Interim final rules should be required to be issued as proposed rules and should automatically expire (proposal: after three years) if the agency does not promulgate a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legislative fix forces agencies to complete notice-and-comment or prevents temporary measures from becoming permanent without full process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce incentives to avoid rulemaking by relieving burdens on informal rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than extending review/requirements to guidance and other nonrule devices, reduce burdens on notice-and-comment to remove incentives to adopt less transparent policymaking vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus reforms on making traditional informal rulemaking more usable (streamlining unnecessary analyses, clarifying expectations for preambles and comment responses) so agencies prefer formal rulemaking when statute requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softer standard of substantive judicial review (the 'pass-fail prof' metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should act like a pass-fail professor—screening out clearly inadequate agency decisions but not demanding the 'best' decision; only inexcusable gaps, obvious misquotes, or intellectual dishonesty should trigger remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider legislative signaling or doctrinal recalibration to reduce intensity of review so agencies are not compelled to document every conceivable analytic contingency; balance this with the risk of administrative arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and focus reform on 'high-stakes' rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossification is most pronounced in 'high stakes' rulemakings—major rules implementing new programs, expanding programs, establishing important precedents, or with large economic consequences—so reforms should account for differing stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor procedural/analytical expectations to the stakes: permit more streamlined processes for low-impact rules and reserve resource-intensive scrutiny for genuine high-stakes decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address the political and strategic expansion of rulemaking participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern rulemaking involves broader actors (advocacy organizations, think tanks, grassroots groups, media, bloggers) and strategic multi-arena tactics that lengthen and politicize rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design oversight, transparency, and procedural rules that anticipate multi-venue strategic behavior and seek to keep deliberation focused on the administrative record and statutory purpose rather than external political gamesmanship.
